name: Rosa Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Rosa, thanks for agreeing to this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We're not linked to AI companies, employers, unions or any party, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say out loud and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right. I'm not much of a talker, so you'll have to bear with me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: That's fine. What's a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a site carpenter for a housebuilder, doing second fix on new estates. That's the work after the plastering: hanging doors, fitting skirting and architraves, putting up the stair spindles, boxing in pipes. Right now we're on a 90-house estate off the bypass, and I'll do maybe six or seven doors on a good day. I like a door that swings and closes on its own with a nice click. I don't like when the plasterers have left the walls out of line and I'm the one who looks bad.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Quiet, mostly. My husband Gareth works nights picking orders at the big distribution warehouse, so I see him at breakfast and that's about it on weekdays. Owen's thirteen, Megan's eight, and they keep me busy. I don't do any of the AI stuff. I've got a phone for calls and the weather and the group chat for the school, and that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, probably, but quietly. I've never thought a computer was going to hang a door. I wouldn't post anything, I don't post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd mean nothing changes, and that suits me. I know what I'm doing. I know where the work comes from. I'd rather not have to learn anything new at this point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Finish this estate, go on to the next one. The firm's got another phase starting in spring, so I'd expect to be there. We'd keep a bit aside each month like we do, nothing different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like the weather forecast said storms and it just drizzled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Gareth's work in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one thing I'd still keep an eye on. They've already put some robots in his warehouse, little ones that bring shelves to the pickers. He says it's made his job easier, not gone. So if that's as far as it goes, we're fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The plasterers. I'm joking, mostly. The usual stuff, you know. Mortgage went up last year, and the price of everything's up. That's not computers, that's just life.

S0.say: I've never thought a computer was going to hang a door, so I wouldn't be surprised. I'd say so quietly at work, but I wouldn't post anything.
S0.think: It means nothing changes, and that suits me. I know the work and where it comes from, and I'd rather not learn anything new at this point.
S0.do: Carries on with second fix on the current estate and moves to the firm's next phase in spring. Keeps saving the same small amount each month as before.
S0.feel: Calm, like a forecast storm that turned out to be drizzle.
S0.quote: I've never thought a computer was going to hang a door.
S0.fieldNote: Rosa is reserved and practical, and she avoids technology on purpose. A plateau confirms her instincts. Her only background worry is her husband's warehouse job, which already has robots. She frames cost-of-living pressure as just life, not anyone's fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, but things change, they always have. My grandad was a cooper making barrels, and that went. I wouldn't be on any side about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be thinking about Gareth more than me. His warehouse is exactly the sort of place they automate first. And if my estates start using factory-made staircases and pre-hung doors even more, there's less for me to do on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, at first, if I'm honest. I'd wait and see how it shakes out. I'd make sure I'm reliable, on time, doing tidy work, so if they cut back they keep me. Maybe I'd put a bit more in savings, if Gareth's hours went down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like there's something on the stairs in the dark and you'd rather not turn the light on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather not turn the light on. What would turning it on look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sitting down with Gareth and asking what his plan is if the warehouse goes. Or asking my boss straight what the firm's planning. I don't do that sort of thing. I just keep my head down and hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the firm offered training on new equipment, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to, yes. I'm not daft. But I wouldn't volunteer. Let the young ones go first and see if it's worth anything.

S1.say: It's a shame, but things change, like my grandad's barrel-making trade did. I wouldn't take a side about it.
S1.think: I'd be thinking about Gareth's warehouse job more than mine, because that's what they automate first. More factory-made stairs and pre-hung doors would mean less for me on site too.
S1.do: Waits to see how things settle, keeps her work tidy and punctual so she's kept on, and adds a little more to savings if her husband's hours drop. Takes training only if it's required.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like sensing something on the stairs in the dark and not wanting to turn the light on.
S1.quote: Like there's something on the stairs in the dark and you'd rather not turn the light on.
S1.fieldNote: Rosa avoids hard conversations and prefers to keep her head down. Her main worry is her husband's job rather than her own. She sees change as nobody's fault, using her grandfather's trade as the example. She would only train if made to, and let younger workers go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what I'd say. Probably that someone should have seen it coming. Not one lot or the other, all of them, the government, the companies. I'd say it to my sister, nobody else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd frighten me. Gareth and me both out of work inside two years, a mortgage, two kids. I've got no idea what else I'd do. I've done this since I was seventeen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything straight off, no holidays, cancel the TV package, Megan's swimming would have to go. We'd try to save every penny we could. If the work dried up, I'd ask my brother Neil, he's got a small fencing business, maybe he'd take me on for a bit. And we'd claim whatever help there was. I wouldn't like it, but you do what you have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, really. Like the floor going from under you. I'd be lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Owen and Megan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, if I could help it. Owen would know anyway, he's sharp. I'd tell Megan we're tightening our belts. I wouldn't want them carrying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fencing would go too, if robots can do hands-on work. Have you thought about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I hadn't. That's what I mean, I don't know what else there is. You'd just grab whatever's going and hope it lasts a bit longer than the last thing.

S2.say: Someone should have seen this coming, and I mean all of them, the government and the companies. I'd say it to my sister and nobody else.
S2.think: It would frighten me, with Gareth and me both out of work inside two years, a mortgage and two kids. I've done this since I was seventeen and have no idea what else I'd do.
S2.do: Cuts holidays, the TV package and her daughter's swimming straight away and saves every penny. Asks her brother for work at his small fencing business if the building work dries up, and claims whatever public help is available.
S2.feel: Sick and lying awake, like the floor dropping away.
S2.quote: You'd just grab whatever's going and hope it lasts a bit longer than the last thing.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture hits Rosa hard because both household incomes go and she has no plan beyond her trade. She spreads the blame evenly and keeps it private. Her fallback, her brother's fencing firm, falls apart when gently questioned, and she admitted she hadn't thought it through. She would shield her children from the worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said before, someone needs to sort it out. Maybe I'd say it a bit more, since there'd be time to do something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's still the end of what I do. But five years, I might be able to stretch it. The houses still need finishing until the robots are actually here, and they won't be on every site on day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, maybe an extra hundred a month, and try to get the credit card paid off. I'd keep working as long as there was work and keep my eye on what the others do. If the firm put on a course for working with the machines, I'd go, but I wouldn't go looking for one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It'd be on my mind every time I saw something about it on the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep your eye on what the others do. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dean, the lead carpenter. He's the type to try everything new. If he went on some course and came back saying it was worth it, I'd probably follow. If he came back moaning, I wouldn't bother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be different in the five-year version for Gareth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd have time to look around, maybe. He's talked about driving lorries before, though I suppose they'd be driving themselves too. I don't know. We'd have to actually talk about it, which we're not good at.

S3.say: Someone needs to sort this out, and with five years there's time to do something. I'd probably say that a bit more often.
S3.think: It's still the end of what I do, but I might stretch it out. Houses still need finishing until the robots arrive, and they won't be on every site on day one.
S3.do: Saves about an extra hundred a month and pays off the credit card. Keeps working while there's work and would join a firm-run course on the new machines, but only if the lead carpenter found it worthwhile.
S3.feel: Anxious, with it on her mind whenever it comes up on the news.
S3.quote: If he went on some course and came back saying it was worth it, I'd probably follow. If he came back moaning, I wouldn't bother.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Rosa hope to stretch her working life rather than change it. She waits for a trusted colleague to test things first. She admits she and her husband don't talk much about hard things. Her anxiety stays steady, and she plans to save but makes no big moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and they'll have to figure something out by then. I'd say that to the lads at work and then talk about the football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I can't really plan that far. I plan in estates, not decades. I'd be 53, the kids would be mostly grown. Part of me thinks something will turn up, it usually does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working and saving. Maybe try to pay a bit extra off the mortgage, if things stay steady. I'd want Owen to think about what he studies, since he'll be leaving school right in the middle of it. Beyond that I'd wait and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more at the back of my mind. It's too far off to keep me up at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Owen to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. He likes computers, which I don't understand at all. I suppose I'd let him decide and just make sure he doesn't end up in something that's going to vanish. Not that I'd know which ones those are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said something usually turns up. Has that been true for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. When the firm I started with went bust, I got on with this one within a month. When Gareth's last place shut, he got the warehouse. So far, it's always worked out. That's maybe why I don't panic. Or why I don't plan.

S4.say: Ten years is a long time, and they'll have to figure something out by then. I'd say that to the lads at work and then talk about football.
S4.think: I can't really plan that far, because I plan in estates, not decades. The kids would be mostly grown, and part of me thinks something will turn up, like it usually does.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving, and overpays the mortgage a little if things stay steady. Talks with her son about what he studies, since he'll leave school in the middle of the change, and otherwise waits to see.
S4.feel: Uneasy but with it at the back of her mind, too far off to keep her awake.
S4.quote: I plan in estates, not decades.
S4.fieldNote: The long warning time lets Rosa push the problem to the back of her mind. She trusts that things tend to work out, based on her own past job losses, and she named the downside herself. Her one forward step is thinking about her son's studies. Otherwise she waits.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, with both of us losing our work at once. What would help? Proper notice, I suppose, and some money to tide you over while you find something. And someone who'd just tell you plainly which jobs are going to last, because I wouldn't know where to start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No, I don't think so. Maybe ask Gareth, he's the one in the warehouse with the robots already. He'd have more to say than me. So far, it's always worked out for us. I'd like it to keep doing that.

headlineQuote: That's maybe why I don't panic. Or why I don't plan.
portrait: Rosa is a 43-year-old second-fix carpenter on new housing estates, married to a night-shift warehouse picker, with two children and a few months of savings. She doesn't use AI and prefers the familiar. In the mild pictures she keeps her head down, and her main worry is her husband's job. The fast AGI picture frightens her because both incomes could go and she has no plan beyond her trade. With more warning time she leans on her belief that something usually turns up, saves a little more and waits to see.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she and her husband would both lose their work at once.
whatWouldHelp: Proper notice, money to tide the family over while she finds something, and someone to tell her plainly which jobs will last.
